task: Frame a decision, check a small data pipeline and use basic statistics and scenarios to recommend a choice.
condition: Given a small data set, pipeline counts, option payoffs and a revenue and cost case.
standard: Row counts reconcile, rates and statistics are correct, a line is fitted, scenarios and break-even are shown and the recommendation names a range.
who: Managers and analysts who must back decisions with data.

modules.title: Framing a decision with numbers
modules.intro: A good decision starts with a clear question, the options, and a measure of success. Without these, data cannot help.
points: State the choice and the deadline
List options and the measure for each
Name what you do not know
modules.example: A firm can launch a product (option A) or wait (option B). A: a 60% chance of a 50,000 gain and a 40% chance of a 10,000 loss. B: a sure 20,000. Expected value of A = 0.6 x 50,000 + 0.4 x (-10,000) = 30,000 - 4,000 = 26,000. B is 20,000. A is higher by 6,000, but A can lose 10,000, so the board checks that it can bear that loss.
modules.activity: Frame a launch decision with two options. Give probabilities and money amounts and work out each expected value.
modules.standard: Expected values are correct for both options and the worst case is stated.

modules.title: Stages of a data pipeline
modules.intro: A pipeline moves data from source to use in stages: collect, clean, store, check and report. Each stage should leave a count.
points: Collect, clean, store, check, report
Count rows in and out of each stage
Keep a log of every rule applied
modules.example: A pipeline starts with 10,000 rows. The clean stage removes 150 duplicates, leaving 9,850. It then removes 200 rows with a missing key, leaving 9,650. The store stage loads 9,650. Check: 10,000 - 150 - 200 = 9,650, so the counts reconcile. If the store had loaded 9,600, 50 rows would be unexplained and the run would stop.
modules.activity: Take a source of 8,000 rows and three clean rules that remove 90, 60 and 25. Compute the rows loaded and write the check.
modules.standard: The loaded count is 7,825 and the check line matches.

modules.title: Data quality checks
modules.intro: Quality checks catch bad data before it reaches a decision. The common checks are completeness, uniqueness, range and timing.
points: Null rate against a limit
Duplicate rate
Range and date checks
modules.example: A table has 400 rows. 12 rows have no region, so the null rate is 12 / 400 = 3%. The limit is 2%, so it fails. 6 rows are exact duplicates, a rate of 1.5%, and the limit is 1%, so it also fails. All 400 sale amounts fall between 0 and 5,000 except 2 rows that show 50,000, which is a likely extra zero. The run is stopped and the source owner is told.
modules.activity: A table has 250 rows, 7 with nulls and 4 duplicates. Compute both rates and compare with 2% and 1% limits.
modules.standard: Rates are 2.8% and 1.6% and both fail the limits.

modules.title: Describing data
modules.intro: Before any model, describe the data with a centre and a spread. The mean, median and standard deviation tell different parts of the story.
points: Mean and median
Spread: standard deviation
Spot outliers
modules.example: Seven daily orders are 4, 6, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14. The total is 60 so the mean is 60 / 7 = 8.57. The median is the middle value, 8. Squared gaps from the mean add to 77.71. Dividing by 6 gives a variance of 12.95, so the standard deviation is 3.6. The mean is close to the median, so no strong skew is shown.
modules.activity: Use six values 3, 5, 5, 7, 9 and 11. Find the mean, median and standard deviation.
modules.standard: Mean is 6.67, median is 6 and the standard deviation is about 2.94, with the working shown.

modules.title: Probability and expected value
modules.intro: Probability measures how likely something is. Conditional probability shows how new evidence changes the odds.
points: Probabilities add to 1
Update with evidence
Expected value is probability times amount
modules.example: 2% of parts are faulty. A test flags 90% of faulty parts and wrongly flags 5% of good parts. Per 1,000 parts: 20 are faulty, 18 of them flagged. Of the 980 good parts, 49 are flagged. Total flags are 67, and 18 / 67 = 26.9% are truly faulty. So even after a flag, the part is faulty only about 1 time in 4, and a second test is needed.
modules.activity: A fault rate is 5%, the test flags 80% of faults and 10% of good parts. Find the chance a flagged part is faulty.

modules.title: Sampling and intervals
modules.intro: A sample lets you judge a large group without counting all of it. An interval shows how sure the estimate is.
points: Standard error is spread divided by the square root of n
A 95% interval is the mean plus or minus 1.96 errors
Larger samples give narrower intervals
modules.example: A sample of 100 customers spends a mean of 52 with a standard deviation of 10. The standard error is 10 / 10 = 1. The 95% interval is 52 plus or minus 1.96, which is 50.04 to 53.96. If the sample was 400, the error would be 10 / 20 = 0.5, and the interval would be 51.02 to 52.98, half as wide.
modules.activity: A sample of 64 has a mean of 80 and a standard deviation of 16. Give the 95% interval.
modules.standard: Standard error is 2, the interval is 76.08 to 83.92.

modules.title: Simple regression and forecasts
modules.intro: A line through points shows how one measure moves with another. The slope is the change in y for each step in x.
points: Slope equals the co-movement divided by the spread of x
The intercept sets the starting level
Do not forecast far outside the data
modules.example: Ad spend x is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (in thousands) and sales y are 3, 5, 6, 9, 12. Mean x is 3 and mean y is 7. The co-movement sum is (-2)(-4) + (-1)(-2) + 0 + (1)(2) + (2)(5) = 8 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 10 = 22. The spread of x is 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 10. The slope is 2.2, the intercept is 7 - 2.2 x 3 = 0.4. Forecast for x = 6 is 0.4 + 13.2 = 13.6.
modules.activity: Fit a line to x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 2, 4, 5 and forecast for x = 4.
modules.standard: Slope is 1.5, intercept is 0.67 and the forecast is 6.67.

modules.title: Sensitivity, scenarios and clear reporting
modules.intro: A forecast is only a guess unless you test what happens when inputs change. Scenarios show which input matters most.
points: Change one input at a time
Find the break-even point
Report ranges, not one figure
modules.example: A project has revenue of 200,000 and costs of 150,000, so profit is 50,000. If revenue falls 10% to 180,000, profit is 30,000, down 40%. If costs rise 10% to 165,000, profit is 35,000, down 30%. Break-even revenue is 150,000, so revenue can fall by 50,000 / 200,000 = 25% before a loss. Revenue is the weaker point, so the report leads with it.
modules.activity: Revenue 120,000, costs 90,000. Test a 10% revenue fall and a 10% cost rise and give the break-even fall.
modules.standard: Profits are 18,000 and 21,000 and the break-even fall is 25%.

quiz.q: Option A gives 70% chance of 10,000 and 30% chance of -5,000. What is its expected value?
A pipeline starts with 5,000 rows, removes 120 and then 80. How many rows load?
12 of 300 rows are null. What is the null rate?
The values 2, 4, 6 have what mean and what median?
1% of items are faulty. A test flags 95% of faults and 4% of good items. Of 1,000, how many flags are good items?
Sample size 25, standard deviation 10. What is the standard error?
Slope is 1.5 and intercept 2. What is the forecast for x = 4?
Revenue is 100,000, costs 80,000. By what percent can revenue fall before a loss?
Why must the count of rows reconcile between stages?
quiz.a: A missing row with no rule to explain it shows data was lost or added by mistake.

quiz.q: Why is a larger sample better for an interval?
quiz.a: The standard error shrinks with the square root of n, so the interval gets narrower.

ladder.title: L1 Basic: Frame the choice
ladder.slide: A slide shows a decision with two options and a number for each.
ladder.notes: Say: no question, no analysis. Check: ask for the measure of success. Mistake: starting with the data instead of the decision.

ladder.title: L2 Basic: Pipeline stages
ladder.slide: Five boxes from collect to report with row counts between them.
ladder.notes: Say: count at every stage. Check: reconcile 10,000 to 9,650. Mistake: trusting a pipeline that gives no counts.

ladder.title: L3 Core: Quality checks
ladder.slide: A table of null rate, duplicate rate and limits with a fail flag.
ladder.notes: Say: stop on a failed check. Check: calculate a rate. Mistake: fixing bad data silently.

ladder.title: L4 Core: Centre and spread
ladder.slide: A set of seven numbers with mean, median and standard deviation worked.
ladder.notes: Say: describe before modelling. Check: find the median. Mistake: using the mean when outliers are present.

ladder.title: L5 Applied: Odds and evidence
ladder.slide: A table of 1,000 parts splits into faulty, good, flagged and not flagged.
ladder.notes: Say: use counts to see the odds. Check: ask the chance after a flag. Mistake: assuming a 90% test means 90% right.

ladder.title: L6 Applied: Intervals and lines
ladder.slide: An interval on a mean and a fitted line with a forecast.
ladder.notes: Say: show the range. Check: widen the interval for a smaller sample. Mistake: forecasting far past the data.

ladder.title: L7 Advanced: Sensitivity and the report
ladder.slide: A scenario table with profit under each change and a break-even line.
ladder.notes: Say: lead with the weakest input. Check: ask for break-even. Mistake: giving one figure with no range.

rubric.meets: Rows in and out reconcile and rates are compared with limits.
rubric.exceeds: Also names the action for each failed check.

rubric.not_yet: Mean, spread or interval is wrong.
rubric.meets: Mean, median, spread and interval are correct.
rubric.exceeds: Also explains what each figure means for the decision.

rubric.meets: Slope, intercept, forecast and conditional odds are correct.
rubric.exceeds: Also warns about the limits of the data.

rubric.meets: Expected values, scenarios and break-even are shown.
rubric.exceeds: Also leads with the weakest input and a clear recommendation.

jobs.what: Cleans data and reports with checks.
Builds expected value and scenario models.
Builds and monitors the data pipeline.
Fits models and tests how sensitive they are.
